 What we covered today
 • Blaming the war: As more House races are projected for Democratic candidates, President Donald Trump said today it was “largely true” the Iran war contributed to the GOP shellacking , echoing remarks from Vice President JD Vance.
 • Possible target: Many Republican lawmakers and allies are moving swiftly to pin blame for the historic losses on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth . And the House could vote as soon as next week to impeach the Pentagon’s top leader.
 • New oversight: Senate Democrats have issued document preservation letters ahead of expected investigations. The Department of Homeland Security is already bracing for an onslaught of congressional oversight efforts , according to current and former officials.
 • What we’re still watching: CNN projects that Democrats will win at least 245 House seats. In the Senate, two contests have not yet been called. CNN Sightline rates the Mississippi race as neutral and Alaska as favoring the Democrat.

 Democrats are still flipping House seats as America waits for the last Senate results
 By Taylor Romine and Hanna Park 
 Bird flies outside the US Capitol on Wednesday. 
 Eric Lee/Reuters 
 As the day after Election Day starts to wind down, many Americans understand Democrats will hold power in Congress, but are now waiting to see how sizable that control will be.
 Results continue to trickle in, with several Democrats flipping House seats across the country and a flip for the GOP. And while there are no final results yet in Mississippi’s Senate race, Democratic candidate Scott Colom told CNN he was feeling “confident.” The emerging majorities are already reshaping Washington’s agenda: Democrats are outlining investigations and promising action on affordability, while Republicans confront divisions over the Iran war and responsibility for their losses.
 Here’s what else is going on in the elections space: 
 Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces mounting pressure as Republican lawmakers and allies are moving to blame him for the party’s historic losses, and the House could vote as soon as next week to impeach him. Florida Gov.-elect Byron Donalds, currently a member of the House, said Wednesday Hegseth is doing his job and he won’t vote to impeach him .
 Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming House Oversight chairman , said Trump investigations won’t distract Democrats from lowering costs, naming four targets: the Trump family’s businesses, immigration enforcement, corporate donations to the White House ballroom, and the Epstein files.
 Florida Governor Ron DeSantis was critical of many Republican races, telling CNN that voters were “disappointed in the productivity” of Congress and playing the blame game on gas prices.
 Across the party aisle, Democratic Senator-elect Annie Andrews also said the Republican party is “fractured,” with the GOP primary between Rep. Ralph Norman and Sen. Darline Graham being a symbol of that rift.
 New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani attributed Democrats win to focusing on working-class Americans and the issues that matter most to them, including cutting costs and building trust with voters.
 Maryland’s Wes Moore used to hold the title of the only Black governor in the US, but soon he will be joined by four others. He emphasized to CNN the historic election of Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms , who is the first Black woman to hold the office.
 Looking ahead, former House Speaker Newt Gingrich put doubt on Vice President JD Vance leading the party as the presidential nominee in 2028, saying the GOP loss in the midterms, along with several strategies Vance has taken, has made “a good bit of the luster has come off the bloom.”
 CNN’s Tori B. Powell, Elise Hammond, Katherine Koretski, Arpita Dasika and Aaron Blake contributed to this report.

 Ford vows to be Nevada’s “most pro-worker” governor after historic win
 By Hanna Park 
 Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford celebrates with attendees during a primary election night watch party in Las Vegas, on June 9. 
 Jae C. Hong/AP 
 Democrat Aaron Ford, who claimed victory in his bid to become Nevada’s first Black governor, cast his win as a triumph for working Nevadans over money and power during a victory speech in Las Vegas on Wednesday.
 “They said it was impossible. They said there was too much money against us,” Ford told supporters. “Last night we proved that your voices matter. We proved that the power belongs to the people. And we won.”
 Ford, the state’s attorney general, said Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo had “graciously conceded” in a phone call earlier that morning. He thanked Lombardo for his willingness to work across partisan divides and pledged to represent Nevadans who voted against him.
 Vowing to tackle affordability “on day one,” he promised to lower the cost of housing, healthcare and energy, guarantee school meals for every child and protect the state’s water. He also pledged to repeal Nevada’s right-to-work law, which prohibits requiring workers to pay union dues or fees as a condition of employment.
 “I intend to be the most pro-worker, pro-union governor this state has ever seen,” Ford said, drawing his loudest applause of the night. “I just firmly believe that a home should be where a family builds a future, not an investment vehicle for Wall Street firms and out-of-state corporations.”
 Recounting his own path from food stamps, Medicaid and Section 8 housing to statewide office, he framed the win as evidence of upward mobility.
 “Don’t let anyone convince you that where you begin decides where you finish.”

 Benitez-Thompson says she has "golden opportunity" to represent rural Nevadans in DC
 By Lex Harvey 
 Teresa Benitez-Thompson poses for a portrait during a campaign event in Incline Village, Nevada, on June 11. 
 Hale Irwin/AP 
 Teresa Benitez-Thompson, Congresswoman-elect for Nevada’s 2nd District, said “frustration across the board” was what drove voters to elect a Democrat to represent her district for the first time.
 The cost of gas was a major pressure point for voters in her largely rural district where many people must drive long distances to access services like health care, Benitez-Thompson told CNN’s Jake Tapper.
 Benitez-Thompson said representing these rural communities in the House is “what’s most important to me,” adding that “taking our rural voices and our community voices to Washington, DC, is going to be very important.”
 “We’ve been handed a golden opportunity, a megaphone for these communities.”
 Benitez-Thompson, who is set to become the first female Hispanic member of the House from her state, said Democrats will do a better job than Republicans at meeting the needs of Latinos.
 “We need to recognize the contributions that everyone in the community brings, fight for everyone, and make sure that policies are lifting families up.”

 Newly elected Democrat says his election is a message of hope by voters
 By Taylor Romine 
 Sam Forstag speaks to students at an event at Montana State University, in Bozeman, Montana on October 23. 
 Robby Brown/AP 
 Democrat Sam Forstag said that voters delivered a message of hope by electing him to Montana’s 1st District, a place President Donald Trump was elected by more than 11 points in 2024.
 Their votes show “that politics should not just be a place where we scream into our cell phone screens about everything that’s wrong with the other party,” Forstag said. “As much as there might be wrong with the party in power right now, it should be a place where we talk about real solutions.”
 Forstag previously worked as a smokejumper, a type of firefighter that jumps into remote areas. That job experience, he said, has prepared him in some ways for his new role.
 “When you get on the ground, whether you’re fighting a fire or framing a house, you don’t ask the person beside you who they voted for last year before you start swinging a tool to fight it,” he said. “You just get to work and get that job done.”

 Hegseth "needs to go," Sen. Mark Kelly says
 By Lex Harvey 
 Arizona Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth needs to “go as soon as possible,” as Republican lawmakers move to blame Hegseth for the Republican Party’s stunning defeat Tuesday.
 “Donald Trump should fire him,” Kelly told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “If he doesn’t fire him, we’ll see what Republicans in the House want to do. It sounds like they want to impeach him. We’ll see what happens with that effort. I would like to see him go as soon as possible because he is just unable to do this job and he’s doing significant damage to the US military.”
 The House could vote as soon as next week to impeach Hegseth, the Pentagon’s top leader.
 Kelly, a retired Navy captain, said once Democrats take control of Congress, they will “put pressure on this president” to end the war in Iran, adding “we’ve got tools.”
 Asked about whether he plans to run for president in 2028, Kelly, who has publicly weighed a White House bid, told Tapper he has not yet made his decision.
 “Right now, I am making a lot of phone calls, congratulating people who won last night,” he said. “I’ll figure the rest of that out later with my family.”

 Garcia insists that future congressional investigations won’t distract from affordability
 By Piper Hudspeth Blackburn 
 Rep. Robert Garcia looks on during a House Oversight and Government Reform Committee hearing in the US Capitol on March 4. 
 Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images 
 The incoming head of the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia, touted the four main investigations the panel will pursue now that Democrats are projected to flip the House, insisting on Wednesday that probes on the “corruption of Donald Trump and this administration” won’t sidetrack efforts to bring down costs.
 “We need to both move forward and pass new laws and lower the costs. There also has to be accountability for the crimes that are being committed because there is a link,” the California lawmaker told reporters at a press conference in Huntington Beach. “If we want to actually bring costs down, then we actually have to take on corruption as well, because it is because the Trumps are enriching themselves.”
 “It’s because the oil companies are enriching themselves,” he continued. “That all goes back to the price of gas. It goes back to the price of groceries because Trump won’t take on the donors and those that are involved in these pricing schemes at the grocery store.”
 Garcia reiterated Democrats will focus on the Trump family’s business dealings, the Department of Homeland Security and its immigration enforcement activities, corporate corruption and donations to the White House ballroom and other monuments in Washington, as well as the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
 CNN previously reported in September that Democrats had already begun to lay the groundwork for investigations if they won control of the House.
 Garcia said Wednesday that Democrats will “be ready on the very first day to launch a series of investigations and actions that will move quickly.”
 CNN’s Annie Grayer contributed to this report.

 Donalds says he won't vote to impeach Hegseth before he leaves Congress 
 1:14
 While Republicans saw losses in the midterm elections, if the party focuses on affordability and prices, the “elections will take care of themselves,” Florida Governor-elect Byron Donalds said.
 “When I was traveling the state of Florida, talking to voters in every county of our state, that was the number one issue on their mind — gas, affordability, housing costs, food,” he told CNN’s Dana Bash. “And I think that as a party, we need to be laser focused on those ideas, on those issues and on lowering those costs for the future of the country.”
 When asked if President Donald Trump did enough in that area, Donalds said “Well, I mean, look, let’s just be very clear. I think $4 gas is $4 gas.”
 He said that was on voters’ minds, and that now the party has the “responsibility now to go back to the drawing board, look at the idea sets, make sure we’re pushing the policies that are going to help people’s lives better.”
 Donalds, currently a member of the U.S. House of Representatives, also weighed in on the possibility of impeaching Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth — a vote that could happen as soon as next week.
 The governor-elect said he won’t vote to impeach Hegseth as Republicans have focused their anger on him. “He is doing his job,” Donalds said.

 Gingrich says Vance is damaged goods in 2028
 Analysis by Aaron Blake 
 At least one prominent Republican seems to think Tuesday’s election results have damaged Vice President JD Vance’s status in the 2028 presidential primaries.
 In an X post , former House Speaker Newt Gingrich says a GOP win would have given Vance “an enormous argument to be the inevitable nominee.”
 But he suggested Vance might have influenced some of the administration’s faulty strategies, including in Iran.
 “Now, with this go-slow strategy blowing up in Iran and his defense of Vivek Ramaswamy’s horrible, inhumane ad featuring his opponent’s mother attacking her own daughter, a good bit of the luster has come off the bloom,” Gingrich said.
 Gingrich hyped Secretary of State Marco Rubio, while also mentioning Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
 Vance is an attractive foil for many in the GOP who don’t seem to have much regard for his policies in the first place — including his non-interventionism and his skepticism of the alliance with Israel. It’s also attractive to blame him rather than President Donald Trump, which Republicans are much more loath to do.
 But there is certainly truth in Gingrich’s comments — that the results hurt Vance’s prospects — which is probably why Vance felt compelled to issue a lengthy explanation of the election results and distanced himself somewhat from Trump’s decisions , again.

 Andrews says South Carolina result shows Republicans rejected Washington-picked candidate

 Democratic Senator-elect Annie Andrews told CNN that a rift between Republicans in her state — and in the country — was a factor in her election.
 She said the GOP primary between Rep. Ralph Norman and Sen. Darline Graham was “a symbol of how fractured the Republican Party is here.”
 Graham defeated Norman in a close runoff this year. Afterwards, Norman revealed to CNN his entire family was not voting for his former opponent, who was hand-picked by President Donald Trump .
 “I also think it’s just a rejection by some Republicans in South Carolina about the idea that Washington would pick our next senator,” she told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on Wednesday night.
 Sen. Darline Graham leaves the stage after giving a speech during an election night watch party in Charleston, South Carolina, on Tuesday. 
 Allison Joyce/Getty Images 
 “As a lot of these Republicans warmed to me in my campaign as they saw me out there hustling, as they understood that I was running to be an independent voice, we were able to bring a lot of them into the coalition. And of course, that’s how we got over 50% of the vote last night,” she said.
 Andrews went on to say that voters in her state have rejected “dirty politics” and that “they wanted something different.”
 “So they took a chance on a mom of three and a pediatrician,” she said.
 “I’m really proud to be the first ever elected female senator from South Carolina.”

 Jace Yarbrough will flip Texas' redrawn 32nd District for the GOP, CNN projects
 By Elise Hammond 
 Jace Yarbrough. 
 From Jace Yarbrough/Facebook 
 Republican Jace Yarbrough, an Air Force veteran and conservative constitutional attorney, will win in Texas’ redrawn 32nd District, CNN’s Decision Desk projects, flipping a Democrat-held House seat.
 The district had been centered around the Dallas suburbs and solidly Democratic. But the 32nd was changed in Republican-led redistricting last year , with its boundaries now stretching east and taking in typically Republican-voting areas.

 Before last night, Wes Moore was the country’s only Black governor . But soon, a record five Black governors will assume office after voters reelected Moore, and chose Keisha Lance Bottoms, Aaron Ford, David Crowley and Byron Donalds for the job.
 Moore told CNN’s Jake Tapper he campaigned so much for other candidates this midterm season “to make sure that no one ever has to hold that title ever again.”
 “For the 250-year history of this country, we’ve had three African Americans elected governor in 250 years. Come January, 10% of the governors in this country will be Black,” Moore said Wednesday. “That’s one election cycle and so this is a pretty remarkable time.”
 One of the candidates Moore campaigned for was Bottoms, who last night became the first Black woman to hold the title in US history.

 Close to 'extinction-level event' for GOP: DeSantis

 The Democratic wave that led the party to take over both chambers of Congress was a result of voters being “disappointed in the productivity” of Congress members, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said, adding they “really didn’t have much to run on.”
 “This was across the country, voters coming out — obviously on the Democrat side, independents and even some crossover Republicans — to express their displeasure about what’s going on in Washington and both sides of Pennsylvania Avenue,” he told CNN’s Jake Tapper.
 The “open-ended” war in Iran had an impact on voters as well, specifically a “direct effect on people’s pocketbooks.”
 “Every time they went to the gas pump, they saw the gas higher,” DeSantis said. “And I’ve criticized some of our Republican congressmen and Senate candidates running around the country trying to blame the high gas prices on Biden. Gas was $3 a gallon a year and a half ago, and now it’s four, and it’s four because of the (Iran) war. So when you gaslight people, they don’t trust you on anything else.”
 The issue of inflation was a problem for Republicans as well, he said, because “when they go to the grocery store, they’re reminded of that and their wages are not keeping up with the costs of living.”
 Looking toward the future of the Republican party, DeSantis advocated for more ideas in the party about what to accomplish and stand for.
